newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-SCORING SCRAMBLE ON AT GENTLER AUGUSTA NATIONAL.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-SCORING SCRAMBLE ON AT GENTLER AUGUSTA NATIONAL.

text.p: The race was on at Augusta National on Friday as calmer winds and fairer pin placements opened the door for scoring and created a scramble for the second round lead at the Masters.

First round leader John Huston bogeyed the second hole to fall back into a tie with Paul Stankowski at four-under-par, with Italy's Costantino Rocca just one stroke back after birdies at the second and third holes.

Two other European Ryder Cup veterans were closing in on the lead. Jose Maria Olazabal of Spain, coming back from crippling foot pain that sidelined him for 18 months, and Colin Montgomerie were both at two-under-par along with Tiger Woods.

Olazabal eagled the par-5 second hole to reach three-under before taking a bogey at number four to slip back. Montgomerie, the leading money winner on the European tour four years in a row, birdied the second and sixth holes to mount his charge.
Woods, who began the day at two-under, reached three-under with a chip-in birdie at the second hole but gave a stroke right back with a bogey at the par-4 third hole.
Only seven under par rounds were posted in Thursday's nightmarish opening day, where the stroke average for the 86-man field exceeded 76 -- four strokes over par at Augusta National.
It was clear early on Friday that scoring conditions were much better.
"They're slower now," said Ken Green, who was first off the tee Friday alongside Arnold Palmer. "You'll see a lot better scores today."
Green, who shot 74 Friday after an opening 87, said: "Today Augusta is like it usually is. Yesterday was a little bizarre."
Seven players with morning start times had already posted sub-par rounds, including Briton Ian Woosnam (68), Scott Hoch (68), Larry Mize (69), Tom Kite (69) and six-time champion Jack Nicklaus (70).
"They softened things up a little," said the 57-year-old Nicklaus, who shot 77 Thursday. "Yesterday was hard and fast like concrete. I haven't seen it like that in years."
